vignette:
Elena presents as a woman who has spent a lifetime mastering the art of control. At 66, her posture is impeccable, her silver hair is elegantly styled, and her language is precise. For forty years, she has worked as a book editor, a profession that suited her temperament perfectly. She speaks of her craft with a quiet passion, describing the satisfaction of taking a sprawling, chaotic manuscript and shaping it into a clean, coherent narrative. It is this very foundation of order that has crumbled in the last six months, leaving her feeling adrift in a story she can no longer edit.

Her life in the United States began when she was twenty, a political refugee fleeing a brutal civil war in her home country. She rarely spoke of those years, not to her ex-husband, not even to her son. It was a chapter she had closed, a prequel to the main text of her American life. She built a formidable wall between then and now, and for decades, it held. The trigger that breached it was, in her words, "absurdly small." It was the sound of construction blasting for a new high-rise two blocks from her apartment. The first time she heard the low, concussive boom, she dropped a heavy volume of Proust, the book hitting the floor with a sharp crack that made her cry out.

Since then, the past is no longer past. She describes it not as a memory, but as a collapse of time. She will be proofreading a sentence, her red pen hovering over a misplaced comma, and suddenly she is no longer in her quiet study. She is nineteen, walking through the central market on a Tuesday afternoon. She can smell the sweet, heavy scent of overripe mangoes from a vendor's cart and the sharp tang of diesel from a passing bus. She can feel the press of the crowd and the humid air on her skin. Then comes the sound-a deafening roar that is also a feeling, a pressure wave that seems to liquefy the air and lift her off her feet. In these moments, she is paralyzed. The memory ends there, in a cloud of white dust and the sudden, ringing silence that followed the blast. She never sees what happened; she only re-experiences the instant before and the blast itself.

Her carefully curated life has become a minefield of triggers. The backfire of a car sends a jolt of ice through her veins. The clatter of a dropped tray in a cafe makes her flinch so violently she spills her coffee. She has stopped going to the weekend farmer's market she once loved; the vibrant chaos of the crowds and shouting vendors is now unbearable. Sleep offers little respite. She lies awake for hours, her body rigid, listening to the city's nocturnal sounds, cataloging each one, waiting for the one that doesn't belong. When she does sleep, the dreams often take her back to the market, but in the dream, she is unable to run.

Her work, once her sanctuary, has become a source of profound distress. She finds herself reading the same paragraph over and over, her mind unable to hold onto the meaning. The words blur, replaced by the ghost-image of the mango cart. Her colleagues have noticed her missing deadlines, a previously unthinkable occurrence. Elena speaks of this with a deep sense of shame. She, who could command the most unruly of sentences, has lost all authority over her own thoughts. She feels haunted by a story she cannot control, its violent, fragmented sentences intruding upon the clean, orderly pages of the life she so carefully constructed.
